preamble: 9 today, hooray, hooray, for 14 across 24 across, Mr 24 down (who appears step-wise in the grid from the middle of 14 down)

clue.text: A lot to eat, but no stomach for it

indicators.note: the stomach is the middle of a word, so the central letter of the eating word is taken away

parts.note: to munch is to eat noisily

explanation.surface: Someone who could eat plenty but has lost their appetite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no stomach for it' removes N, the middle letter of MUNCH.
explanation.definitionFit: Much and a lot are interchangeable quantity words, as in 'drinks much' or 'drinks a lot'.

clue.text: Swindle detected in Cameron's campaign

indicators.note: the letters are found sitting inside the run of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A fraud uncovered in a political leader's election campaign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'detected in' points into Cameron's campaign, where the run is spread across the end of one word and the start of the next.
explanation.definitionFit: A scam is a confidence trick, a straightforward synonym for a swindle.

clue.text: See 10
Author bearing fruit as 24 across

indicators.note: the author's name carries the fruit inside it, as a tree bears fruit

parts.note: Stephen King is the American horror novelist
a haw is the red berry of the hawthorn

explanation.surface: A writer who is as brilliant as a fruitful tree is productive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bearing' is not carrying in the sense of direction: the horror novelist's name holds the berry, and the surname splits round it.
explanation.definitionFit: Stephen Hawking, the Cambridge cosmologist, is a standard example of a scientific mastermind.

clue.text: Funny nun done one (nudge nudge, wink wink …

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: something funny is odd or out of shape, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A comic line about a nun having 'done one', delivered with a knowing nudge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Funny' rearranges NUN, DONE and I (one). 'Nudge nudge, wink wink' is the Monty Python catchphrase for a saucy hint.
explanation.definitionFit: The catchphrase is the classic signal of a sly suggestive remark, which is exactly what an innuendo is.

clue.text: Still available to accommodate the German, as promised

indicators.note: the first word makes room for the second inside it

parts.note: something untaken has not been claimed and is still available
der is a German word for the

explanation.surface: A room still free to house a German guest, just as was agreed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as' links the wordplay to the definition, which is the past participle of undertake in its sense of pledge.
explanation.definitionFit: A task undertaken is one pledged or agreed to, so the word works as promised.

clue.text: "Lusty swings" describing attack over dull mind

indicators.note: to describe is to draw round, so the rearranged letters surround the other piece
the word lusty swings about, its letters rearranged
in a down clue over means turned upside down, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: a fit is a sudden attack, of coughing say

explanation.surface: A lusty dance swinging round a fit that dulls the brain.
explanation.walkthrough: Lusty swings rearranges to STULY; 'over' turns the fit backwards in this down clue, and 'describing' means drawing a line round it.
explanation.definitionFit: To stultify is to make the mind dull and sluggish, a verb phrase meaning the same thing.

clue.text: Drink problem reversed, one training for the police

indicators.note: the word for the problem is turned round

parts.note: a sum is an arithmetic problem
a police cadet is a trainee officer

explanation.surface: A trainee officer with a drink problem that has been turned round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reversed' turns SUM into MUS. Muscadet is a dry white wine from the Loire.
explanation.definitionFit: Muscadet is a white wine, so it is one kind of drink.

clue.text: New order in yet? Ten of these

indicators.note: a new order rearranges the letters

explanation.surface: Asking whether a fresh order has come in yet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'order' rearranges N, IN and YET. 'these' refers to the clue's own number, 9: ten nines make the number.
explanation.definitionFit: Ten lots of the clue number nine add up to the number of the Guardian setter's birthday.

clue.text: Head of Operations in the Mossad going walkabout with 24 across

indicators.note: the letters wander off and come back in a new order
the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: The head of operations in the Israeli intelligence service goes missing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head of' takes O from Operations; 'going walkabout' rearranges O, IN and THE MOSSAD. The Mossad is Israel's intelligence agency.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Edison, inventor of the phonograph and practical light bulb, is a byword for inventive brilliance.

clue.text: Alternative resistance from the Guardian columnist

parts.note: or introduces an alternative
R is the symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: A dissenting view from someone who writes for the paper.
explanation.walkthrough: Deborah Orr was a columnist for the Guardian.
explanation.definitionFit: Deborah Orr wrote a regular column for the Guardian, the newspaper that ran this puzzle.

clue.text: She's breaking rule with dodgy plan

indicators.note: breaking the rule smashes its letters into a new order
a dodgy plan is unsound, so its letters are rearranged too

explanation.surface: A woman who breaks the rules with a shady scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaking' and 'dodgy' together rearrange RULE and PLAN into a woman's name, as in Prunella Scales.
explanation.definitionFit: Prunella is a female given name, so it can stand in for a woman referred to as she.

clue.text: I say nothing I see

parts.note: O is the figure zero, nothing
oh is said on understanding, like 'I see'

explanation.surface: Someone keeping quiet about what they have noticed.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are exclamations of surprise or delight, so one can replace the other.

clue.text: Worn out — almost shattered — by the local community

indicators.note: shattered letters are broken up and reassembled
almost means the word is cut short by its final letter

explanation.surface: Feeling worn out and nearly shattered by the neighbours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' trims OUT to OU; 'shattered' rearranges WORN and OU.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means people who belong to us, the home crowd, which is what a local community is.

clue.text: Blade slicing head off pig

indicators.note: the first letter of the animal's name is cut away

parts.note: a boar is a male pig

explanation.surface: A butcher's knife lopping the head off a pig.
explanation.walkthrough: 'slicing head off' removes B from BOAR.
explanation.definitionFit: The flat end of an oar is called its blade, and blade is also a poetic term for the whole oar.

clue.text: 24 across Mark Twain's odd characters ignored line in composition

indicators.note: the pieces sit inside the poem

parts.note: an ode is a poetic composition
a scar is a mark left on the skin

indicators.note: only the even letters of the author's surname are kept, skipping first, third and fifth

explanation.surface: A clue about Mark Twain's stray letters and a line in a piece of writing.
explanation.walkthrough: Mark Twain looks like one name, but it splits: Mark is a scar and only Twain's even letters survive.
explanation.definitionFit: Oscar Wilde, the Irish playwright and wit, is a stock example of literary brilliance.

clue.text: See 28
Harsh half of 15 confused with Ulster Unionist

indicators.note: the letters are muddled together
half of the cross-referenced name is its first word

parts.note: 15 down is the Irish playwright's full name
UU is the abbreviation for Ulster Unionist

explanation.surface: Harsh words as half of a famous wit is muddled with a Northern Irish politician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half of' takes OSCAR from 15's answer; 'confused' rearranges OSCAR and UU. Ulster Unionists are a Northern Irish political party.
explanation.definitionFit: A raucous sound is loud and grating, which is what harsh means of a voice.

clue.text: Objectors adopting URL, say, of Fantasy Island

indicators.note: the objectors take the example into their midst

parts.note: antis are people opposed to something
URL is an example of a three-letter acronym, abbreviated TLA

explanation.surface: Protesters taking up the web address of a television fantasy island.
explanation.walkthrough: Fantasy Island was an American TV series, but here it simply describes the legendary sunken island.
explanation.definitionFit: Atlantis is the legendary island said to have sunk beneath the sea, an imaginary place.

clue.text: Using mobile you arrest an unruly adolescent with no subsidence

parts.note: in mobile text messaging, you is written as the single letter U
to nab is to arrest
an gives the letter A
a Ted is a Teddy boy, a rowdy 1950s youth

explanation.surface: Someone on their phone collaring a delinquent teenager.
explanation.walkthrough: Teddy boys were 1950s British youths known for Edwardian-style dress and rowdy behaviour.
explanation.definitionFit: Unabated means without lessening, so it fits a phrase about something that has not subsided.

clue.text: Sums involving grand, or halves thereof

indicators.note: the sums enclose the grand

parts.note: moneys are sums of cash
K stands for a thousand, a grand

explanation.surface: Sums of money involving thousands or so.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involving' puts K inside MONEYS. In British slang a monkey is £500, half a grand.
explanation.definitionFit: A monkey is slang for five hundred pounds, which is half of a thousand.

clue.text: Possible message from holed ship?

parts.note: a sinking vessel would radio for help, and the ship's letters can be read with a hole punched in their middle

explanation.definitionFit: The Morse distress call is what a stricken vessel sends to summon rescue.

clue.text: See 4
QE1 struggling along, negotiating water-filled valley

indicators.note: to negotiate a valley is to get round it, so the letters go around it
the letters struggle into a new order

parts.note: a ria is a drowned river valley

explanation.surface: Queen Elizabeth I struggling along through a flooded valley.
explanation.walkthrough: Along struggles into GLONA, and 'negotiating' has it work its way round the drowned valley.
explanation.definitionFit: Gloriana was the poetic name given to Queen Elizabeth I, notably by Spenser.

clue.text: Foremost of intellects in class

indicators.note: the letter goes inside the class

parts.note: a genus is a class in biological ordering

indicators.note: the foremost part of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: The brightest minds in a group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foremost of' gives I from intellects; 'in' puts it inside GENUS. The whole clue also defines.
explanation.definitionFit: A genius stands at the top of the intellects, in a class of their own.

clue.text: Eureka! Cracked sources of Great Reverend Master!

definitions.text: Eureka! Cracked sources of Great Reverend Master!

indicators.note: the initials are cracked open and the cry put inside
the sources of words are their first letters

parts.note: aha is a cry of discovery like Eureka

explanation.surface: A cry of discovery as the great reverend master finally works it out.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation 'Eureka!' supplies the cry, not the definition: the preamble names the Rev John Graham, the setter Araucaria, turning 90.
explanation.definitionFit: Read whole, the clue salutes the Reverend John Graham, the setter Araucaria, as a great master who cracks puzzles, so it describes the man.

clue.text: Diamonds, that is, capturing clubs

indicators.note: the first piece takes the second inside

parts.note: ie is the abbreviation for id est, that is
C is the card abbreviation for clubs

explanation.surface: A card game where diamonds take the clubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capturing' puts C between I and E.
explanation.definitionFit: Ice is slang for diamonds, from their glittering clear look.

clue.text: Greenback from Mars?

parts.note: read as green with its word turned back, and as what Mars, the god, brings

explanation.definitionFit: Mars was the Roman god of conflict, so armed conflict is what comes from him.

clue.text: An imposing character — one of Kafka's — producing type of missile

parts.note: taken as written
a titan is a figure of great size or power
Josef K. is the protagonist of Kafka's The Trial

explanation.surface: A towering figure from a Kafka novel producing a weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one of Kafka's' looks like a letter of the name but is his character K.
explanation.definitionFit: An antitank missile is designed to destroy armoured vehicles, so the word describes a kind of missile.

clue.text: Blare out "2 x (10 ÷ 1)", captivating second 24 across

indicators.note: out means the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the pair of pieces holds the S between them
two times means the piece appears twice
dividing ten by one is read as splitting it with the numeral

parts.note: ten in words
one as the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A loud formula-like sum blared out, capturing a genius.
explanation.walkthrough: Blare out rearranges to ALBER; the arithmetic is read in words, with '÷' splitting ten by the Roman one and '2 x' doubling the result.
explanation.definitionFit: Albert Einstein, author of relativity, is the archetypal example of supreme intelligence.

clue.text: Danish physicist locating pong on time

parts.note: BO is body odour, a pong
HR is the abbreviation for hour, a unit of time

explanation.surface: Locating a famous physicist by the smell and the hour.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' places the time after the smell.
explanation.definitionFit: Niels Bohr was a Danish physicist known for his model of the atom.

clue.text: Bloody right — time to get up!

indicators.note: in a down clue getting up reverses the word, reading it from bottom to top

parts.note: an era is a period of time

explanation.surface: An alarm-clock exclamation: right, time to get out of bed!
explanation.walkthrough: 'to get up' reverses ERA to ARE. 'Bloody' is a British exclamation, but here it describes steak.
explanation.definitionFit: A rare steak is red inside and bloody, so the words match of meat.

clue.text: Pervade conundrum

definitions.meaning: to spread through, as bullets or errors fill something

explanation.definitionFit: The word is a verb meaning to fill throughout and a noun meaning a puzzling question.

clue.text: A horse tender? Strangely not!

indicators.note: the letters are arranged strangely

parts.note: H is slang for heroin, known as horse

explanation.surface: Asking whether someone tends horses, and being told no.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strangely' rearranges A, H and TENDER. A neatherd tends cattle (neat is an old word for cattle), not horses.
explanation.definitionFit: A neatherd is a cowherd, a tender of cattle rather than horses.
